title: House of the Dragon Returns June 21 With a Perfect 100% Score. Indian Fans Get the War One Day Later on JioHotstar.
excerpt: After a two-year wait and a divisive Season 2 finale, the Dance of the Dragons finally erupts into all-out war — and critics are calling it a return to form. Here's when and where the diaspora can watch.
body:
Westeros has been holding its breath for nearly two years. The Season 2 finale of **House of the Dragon** ended not with fire and blood but with a frustrating stillness — armies massing, dragons grounded, everyone glaring at maps. Fans wanted the war. On **June 21**, they finally get it.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=0JlMjgqduVw</youtube>

**House of the Dragon Season 3** premieres on **HBO and HBO Max** at 9 PM ET on Sunday, June 21, and for Indian viewers it lands on **JioHotstar from June 22** — a one-day gap that, in the age of instant spoilers, the diaspora has learned to survive. New episodes drop weekly, eight in all, with the finale set for **August 9**. If you've been waiting since 2024 to find out who burns and who survives, the countdown is finally measured in days, not seasons.

And the early word is staggering. Ahead of the premiere, Season 3 debuted with a **perfect 100% on Rotten Tomatoes** across the first batch of critic reviews — a series record, comfortably ahead of Season 1's 90% and Season 2's 84%. After a sophomore run that left many viewers cold, that number reads like a course correction. Screen Rant called it the moment "Game of Thrones finally masters neck-breaking momentum," praising a pacing overhaul that finally lets the story breathe and bleed.

> "If you liked the first two seasons of House of the Dragon, you'll like Season 3 more. At least it's not boring. The explosive part of the plot is here, at last." — New York Post review

Not everyone is fully converted. The Post's reviewer noted the season "whips around so jerkily" between battles that it occasionally dulls the emotional punch, and Screen Rant flagged the show's persistent struggle whenever it strays from **George R.R. Martin**'s *Fire & Blood* source material — the non-canon Sheepstealer subplot singled out as the weakest thread. But the consensus is clear: this is the most alive the show has felt since the pilot.

The cast that made the show a phenomenon is all back. **Emma D'Arcy** returns as Rhaenyra Targaryen, the queen who would burn the realm to keep her claim. **Matt Smith** is back as the dangerous, magnetic Daemon, and **Olivia Cooke** returns as Alicent Hightower, whose quiet betrayals have driven the whole tragedy. **Ewan Mitchell**'s Aemond — arguably the breakout villain of the series, all cold menace and that single sapphire eye — continues opposite **Tom Glynn-Carney**'s wounded, paranoid Aegon II. New blood arrives too: **James Norton** joins as Ormund Hightower, with **Tommy Flanagan** and **Dan Fogler** rounding out the expanding war.

What's actually coming? The Dance of the Dragons — the brutal Targaryen civil war that the entire series has been building toward — reaches its critical points. Season 3 "will see the realm break into all-out war and devastating blows," with the conflicts that simmered through Season 2 finally boiling over. The cast hasn't minced words: one described the premiere battle in terms of "pain" and "bloodlust chaos." For a show whose currency is dragon-on-dragon spectacle, that is a promise, not a warning.

For the Indian diaspora, the *Game of Thrones* universe has always punched far above its niche. The original series turned Sunday-night watch parties into a global ritual, and HOTD inherited that fervour — the WhatsApp group threads, the spoiler-dodging, the Monday-morning post-mortems stretching from Bengaluru to Brampton. JioHotstar's near-simultaneous release means an NRI in California and a fan in Mumbai can argue about the same dragon death within hours of each other. The franchise also carries a quiet desi badge of honour: Ramin Djawadi's iconic theme aside, this is appointment television that crosses every cultural line a diaspora household contains.

A practical note for cord-cutters abroad: outside India, HOTD lives exclusively behind an HBO Max subscription (from $10.99/month with ads). Inside India, JioHotstar carries it. Either way, the weekly format is back — no binge, no shortcuts, just eight Sundays of slow-burn dread.

Two years is a long time to wait for a war. On June 21, the dragons stop posturing and start fighting. Clear your Sunday nights through August — and maybe mute a few group chats until you've caught up.
